# The Man Led by a Woman {#the-man-led-by-a-woman}

> "He followed her immediately, as an ox goes to the slaughter"
>
> — Proverbs 7:22

There's a man you may recognize at any party. He walks in and goes straight to the women. He doesn't say hello to the men. He buys a round, and every glass goes to a girl. He would tell you he is just a generous, friendly guy.

Here is the test. Does he buy the men a drink? Does he spend as much time talking to the men? A generous man is generous with everybody. This man is spending, and he knows what he is shopping for. What makes the difference is what he intends.

The slang of the 2020s calls it simping. The word is new. The problem is very old, and it comes down to one sentence.

**A man ruled by what he wants ends up ruled by whoever can give it to him.**

Think of his wanting as a lever that sticks out of him. Anyone who takes hold of it can move him. This chapter is about that lever: who pulls it, how old the trick is, and what a man looks like once it is gone.

## The man who waits {-}

The man at the bar is the loud kind. There is a quiet kind, and there are far more of him.

He has a friend, she is a woman, and he has been in love with her for three years. He drives her to the airport. He fixes her computer. He listens for an hour while she talks about the man she is actually seeing. He calls it friendship.

But a friend wants nothing back, and this man is keeping count. Every favor is a payment into an account that he believes will pay out one day. She may know it and enjoy the service. She may have no idea. Either way, he isn't being kind to her. He is waiting to be paid. And under the good manners he is angry that the payment hasn't come.

Put the same test to him. Would he do all this for a man? Would he do it for her if he knew for certain that nothing would ever come of it? If the answer is no, it was never a gift.

## Whoever knows what he wants {-}

The lever doesn't care whose hand is on it. A woman can pull it, and so can anyone else who knows what he wants.

The man who makes advertisements knows. That is why a pretty girl is leaning on the car. The stranger who writes to him out of nowhere knows. In her pictures she is young and lovely, and she thinks he is wonderful, and after three weeks she has a trouble that only his money can fix. Very often "she" is a man at a desk, working from a script. Governments know it too. For as long as there have been secrets, the cheapest way to get one has been to send a pretty woman to the man who keeps it.

None of these people is stronger or cleverer than he is. They don't need to be. They only need to know where the lever is.

## The strongest man who ever lived {-}

None of this is new. The oldest full account of it is in the Bible, in the book of Judges, and it is about a man named Samson. He was the strongest man who ever lived. God gave him that strength to free his people from their enemies, the Philistines, and no army could hold him. His weakness was women, and his enemies knew it. He fell in love with a woman named Delilah, and the Philistine rulers came to her with an offer. "Entice him, and see in which his great strength lies." Each of them promised her eleven hundred pieces of silver.

Three times she asked him for his secret. Three times he told her a lie, and each time she tried it on him with armed men hiding in the next room.

Stop there and look at him. Three times this woman has tried to hand him to men who want him dead. He knows it. And he stays. That is what lust does to a strong man's judgment. He isn't fooled. He just can't leave.

Then she used the oldest line there is. "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me?" She "pressed him daily with her words" until he was worn out, and at last he told her the truth. His strength was tied to a vow of dedication to God, and its sign was that his hair had never been cut. She put him to sleep on her knees, called a man to shave his head, and collected her silver.

He woke up sure that he would shake himself free as before. "But he didn't know that the LORD had departed from him." The Philistines put out his eyes, the eyes that had led him all his life, "and he ground at the mill in the prison".

That is not quite the end. His hair grew again, and on his last day, blind and brought out to be laughed at, he prayed, and God heard him. A ruined man can still be heard. But he never got back his sight, or the wasted years.

Notice where the story puts the blame. Delilah sold him for silver, and that was treachery. But nobody took his secret from him. He gave it away.

## The king who turned his face to the wall {-}

Samson was led by a woman he wanted. The second man is a quieter case, and more men are like him. He was a king named Ahab, and his wife was Jezebel.

Ahab wanted a vineyard that lay next to his palace. The owner, a man named Naboth, wouldn't sell. The land had been in his family for generations. So the king went home. He "laid himself down on his bed, and turned away his face, and would eat no bread." He was a grown man and a king, and he sulked like a child because someone had told him no.

Jezebel found him there. "Do you now govern the kingdom of Israel?" she said. "Arise, and eat bread, and let your heart be merry. I will give you the vineyard". Then she "wrote letters in Ahab's name, and sealed them with his seal". The letters arranged for Naboth to be accused of a crime he had not committed and stoned to death.

Ahab asked no questions. He didn't ask what she meant to do, or how the vineyard had suddenly come free. When she told him Naboth was dead, he got up and went down to take it.

Jezebel was a murderer, and the Bible doesn't spare her. But it was his name on the letters and his seal in the wax. He didn't lend them because he was afraid of her. He lent them because she was getting him what he wanted, and a man who is being given what he wants doesn't ask how. The Bible's verdict on him is that he "sold himself".

Mark Driscoll, an American pastor, gives the men of his church a short rule drawn from that marriage: "If you tolerate, they will dominate." Ahab tolerated everything, because his silence had been paid for.

There is a simple way to find out whether you are Ahab. Say no to something, kindly and plainly, and see what it costs you. If you already know what it will cost, and that is why you haven't said it in years, then someone has a hand on the lever.

## The free man in the room {-}

So what does a man look like with the lever gone? Put him in a room full of women, at any party.

He can see that a woman is beautiful. It simply stops deciding anything. He doesn't buy the drink or laugh at the joke that wasn't funny. He doesn't give her the favor, the job or the last word because of her face. He treats her as he treats everyone else, which is fairly.

That is better for him. He keeps his money, his judgment and his self-respect. It is better for her too, because she gets dealt with as a person. And it is better for the plain woman standing beside her, whom thirsty men have looked straight through all her life.

## The lever at home {-}

It matters far more with the woman he lives with. Ahab's silence was bought with a vineyard. In most houses it is bought with something else.

There's a man who gives in on everything. When his partner is unfair to him, or plainly out of line, he says nothing, because he is afraid of what it will cost him that night. Sex has become a lever in that house. Some women pull that lever on purpose, and that is wrong of them. Others never give it a thought. But he can't change her. What he can change is whether the lever works.

Now take the man whose lust no longer runs him. He can say, quite calmly, "That isn't right, and I won't go along with it." If she tells him he can sleep on the couch tonight, he picks up a pillow and goes. To him it feels like camping.

He isn't being cold, and he isn't punishing her. He still loves her, and he still wants her. But he can't be bought with it, and he can't be starved with it, so he is free to tell her the truth. That is better for her as well. She can trust his yes, because he is a man who is able to say no.

Samson was the strongest man alive, and Ahab was a king, and neither of them could say no. The man with the pillow under his arm is neither strong nor a king. He is only free, and that turns out to be the one thing that matters. Nobody can lead him by what he wants, because it no longer leads him.
